questions.question: A bar model is cut into 10 equal parts. 4 of the parts are shaded green and the other 6 parts are white. Writing the shaded parts as a part-to-whole ratio, which line shows that ratio as a fraction, a decimal and a percent?
questions.explain: Part-to-whole means shaded parts over ALL the parts: 4 out of 10, so 4/10 = 0.4 = 40%. The trap is comparing shaded to white (4 to 6) — that is a part-to-part ratio, not part-to-whole.

questions.question: A bar model is cut into 5 equal parts. 3 parts are shaded blue and 2 parts are left empty. Which line writes the blue part-to-whole ratio correctly as a fraction, a decimal and a percent?
questions.explain: The whole bar is all 5 parts, so blue to whole is 3/5, and 3 divided by 5 = 0.6 = 60%. Two traps: comparing blue to empty (3 to 2), and copying the digits 3 and 5 to make 0.35 instead of dividing.

questions.question: A bar model is cut into 8 equal parts. 2 parts are shaded red and 6 parts are unshaded. Which line shows the red part-to-whole ratio as a fraction, a decimal and a percent?
questions.explain: Red to whole is 2 out of the 8 equal parts: 2/8 = 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%. The common trap is writing 2 to 6 (red compared to unshaded), which is part-to-part, not part-to-whole.

questions.question: A bar model is cut into 4 equal parts. 3 parts are shaded yellow and 1 part is white. Which line writes the yellow part-to-whole ratio as a fraction, a decimal and a percent?
questions.explain: Yellow to whole is 3 out of 4 parts: 3/4 = 0.75 = 75%. Watch two traps — comparing yellow to white (3 to 1), and flipping the ratio to 4/3, which makes a number bigger than 1 even though only part of the bar is shaded.

questions.question: In a Grade 7 class of 20 students, 12 students ride the bus to school and 8 students walk. Which line writes the part-to-whole ratio of bus riders to the whole class as a fraction, a decimal and a percent?
questions.explain: Bus riders to the whole class is 12 out of 20, so 12/20 = 3/5 = 0.6 = 60%. The trap is using 12 to 8 (bus riders compared to walkers) — that is part-to-part; the whole is always all 20 students.

questions.question: Priya has 15 hockey cards in a binder. 5 of them show goalies and the other 10 show skaters. Which line writes the part-to-whole ratio of goalie cards to all the cards as a fraction, a decimal and a percent?
questions.explain: Goalies to all cards is 5 out of 15 = 1/3, and 1 divided by 3 gives the repeating decimal 0.333..., or about 33.3%. The trap is 5 to 10, which compares goalies to skaters (part-to-part) instead of to the whole binder.

questions.question: A pizza at a birthday party is cut into 8 equal slices. 7 slices are eaten and 1 slice is left. Which line writes the part-to-whole ratio of eaten slices to the whole pizza as a fraction, a decimal and a percent?
questions.explain: Eaten slices to the whole pizza is 7 out of 8: 7 divided by 8 gives the terminating decimal 0.875 = 87.5%. The trap is 7 to 1, which compares eaten slices to the leftover slice rather than to the whole pizza.

questions.question: A school cabinet holds 20 water bottles. 9 of them are blue and 11 are green. Which line writes the part-to-whole ratio of blue bottles to all the bottles as a fraction, a decimal and a percent?
questions.explain: Blue to whole is 9 out of 20; since 20 goes into 100 five times, 9/20 = 45/100 = 0.45 = 45%. The trap is 9 to 11, which compares blue to green (part-to-part) instead of blue to all 20 bottles.

questions.question: A bag holds 20 apples: 12 are green and 8 are red. Jayden says, 'Green apples are 12 to 8, so as a fraction that is 12/8 = 1.5 = 150% of the bag.' Is he right?
options: No — he flipped it; it should be 8 over 12, so 8/12 = 0.66... = about 66.7%.
Yes — green compared with red is 12 to 8, so 12/8 = 1.5 = 150% of the bag.
No — the part-to-whole ratio is 12 to 20, so 12/20 = 3/5 = 0.6 = 60%.
No — it should be the 8 red over all 20 apples, so 8/20 = 0.4 = 40%.
questions.explain: Jayden compared green to red, which is part-to-part; for part-to-whole the bottom number must be all 20 apples, giving 12/20 = 0.6 = 60%. A quick check: one part of a bag can never be more than 100% of it, so any answer over 100% signals a part-to-part mix-up.

questions.question: A box has 30 granola bars for a class hike: 6 are chocolate, 9 are berry, and the rest are oat. Which line writes the part-to-whole ratio of oat bars to the whole box as a fraction, a decimal and a percent?
questions.explain: First find the oat bars: 30 - 6 - 9 = 15, then compare to the whole box: 15/30 = 1/2 = 0.5 = 50%. The trap is comparing oat bars to the 15 non-oat bars, which is part-to-part and wrongly gives 100%.

questions.question: Leo's class has a fundraising goal of $80 for a field trip. They raised $30 on Saturday and $20 on Sunday. Which line writes the part-to-whole ratio of money raised so far to the goal as a fraction, a decimal and a percent?
questions.explain: Add the two days first: $30 + $20 = $50 raised out of the $80 goal, so 50/80 = 5/8 = 0.625 = 62.5%. The trap is comparing the $50 raised to the $30 still needed — that is part-to-part, and it gives more than 100% of a goal you have not reached.

questions.question: For a math project, four students each wrote a part-to-whole ratio and changed it into a decimal. Which of these part-to-whole ratios becomes a repeating decimal instead of a terminating decimal?
questions.explain: Divide the part by the whole: 2 divided by 3 = 0.666..., a repeating decimal (about 66.7%), while 1:4 = 0.25, 3:8 = 0.375 and 7:10 = 0.7 all stop. The trap is guessing from the size of the numbers — what matters is whether the division ends.
